title: Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism: List of current qualifying carbon pricing schemes
key_claim: HMRC published a list of overseas carbon pricing schemes that qualify for carbon price relief under the UK CBAM, based on information available as of 19 June 2026. The named schemes include the EU ETS, China National Emissions Trading System, the Indian Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, Japan GX-ETS, Korea K-ETS, the Australia Safeguard Mechanism, Canada's Federal OBPS, Kazakhstan, Montenegro, New Zealand, Switzerland, Taiwan and carbon taxes in Chile, Serbia, Singapore and South Africa. Relief depends on the effective carbon price paid; emissions covered by free allowances earn no relief, and rebates or refunds reduce the amount claimable.
frame_summary: HMRC is arguing that a published, jurisdiction-level list of qualifying schemes, kept under review and open to engagement from countries whose schemes are still in development, is the workable way to prevent double taxation while preserving the environmental integrity of the UK border charge.
verbatim_quote: Emissions covered by free allowances do not qualify for relief because no effective carbon price has been paid on them.
verbatim_list: The list is based on the information available as of 19 June 2026 and will be updated as further schemes are assessed.

The UK plays an active role in supporting the development of carbon pricing schemes across the world, partly through our participation in Partnership for Market Implementation, and welcomes engagement on how carbon pricing schemes currently under development could meet the criteria for carbon price relief under the CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism).
The amount of relief that can be claimed will depend on the effective carbon price the good has been subject to.

title: The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (Calculation of CBAM Rate and Determination of Carbon Price Relief) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/809)
date_evidence: Made13th July 2026 Laid before the House of Commons14th July 2026 Coming into force1st January 2027
key_claim: The statutory instrument underpinning UK carbon price relief was made on 13 July 2026, laid before the Commons on 14 July 2026 and comes into force on 1 January 2027. Regulation 6 defines qualifying carbon pricing schemes; Part 4 requires verification and accreditation; Part 5 places responsibility for calculating the effective carbon price and the relief due on the importer.
frame_summary: The Treasury and HMRC are arguing that carbon price relief should be a rules-based entitlement fixed in secondary legislation, with the scheme-qualification test, the verification duty and the calculation burden all specified before the border charge starts.

title: Carbon price paid in Third Countries
key_claim: DG TAXUD published the synopsis report on the call for evidence for the CBAM implementing act on the carbon price paid in third countries, and in May 2026 published the implementing act itself for a four-week public feedback period. The consultation covered proof of payment, currency conversion and the eligibility of third-party certifiers.
frame_summary: The Commission is arguing that converting a foreign carbon cost into a reduction of CBAM liability is a technical and evidentiary problem to be solved consignment by consignment, through proof of payment and third-party certification, rather than by publishing a list of approved jurisdictions.
verbatim_quote: This specific consultation aimed at gathering stakeholders' input on the technical and administrative aspects related to the conversion of foreign carbon costs into a reduction of the CBAM liability, including proof of payment, currency conversion, and the eligibility of third-party certifiers.
verbatim_list: In May 2026, the Commission published the implementing act for a 4-week public feedback.

title: Recognizing Third-Country Carbon Prices Under the European CBAM: Options to Close the Price Gap (CEEPR RC-2026-04)

Recognizing Third-Country Carbon 
Prices Under the European CBAM: 
Options to Close the Price Gap
Carolyn Fischer and Michael Mehling
key_claim: Carolyn Fischer and Michael Mehling argue that how Article 9 of the CBAM Regulation is implemented will determine whether the mechanism keeps catalysing carbon pricing abroad, and that a working draft of the implementing regulation was released by the European Commission on 13 May 2026.
frame_summary: The authors are arguing that the recognition rule, not the border charge itself, is the lever through which the EU shapes carbon pricing outside its borders, so the implementing act should be designed for symmetry with the EU ETS while leaving enough flexibility to close the price gap.
verbatim_quote: Article 9 of the CBAM Regulation (Regulation 2023/956) allows importers to claim a reduction in CBAM certificate obligations if they can prove a carbon price was already paid in the country of origin. How this provision is implemented will determine whether the mechanism continues to catalyze carbon pricing abroad, arguably its most consequential climate impact.
verbatim_list: A working draft of the implementing regulation was released by the European Commission on 13 May 2026.

title: Türkiye unveils regulation for its national emissions trading system
key_claim: Türkiye published secondary regulations for its national emissions trading system in the Official Gazette on 27 August 2026. The system covers Category B installations of 50,000 to 500,000 tCO2e and Category C installations above 500,000 tCO2e, sets an intensity-based cap ex post, allocates allowances free and by auction, and introduces a complementary carbon price mechanism allowing entities to pay voluntarily above the auction price.
frame_summary: ICAP is arguing that Türkiye's regulation is a deliberate act of alignment with the EU ETS and CBAM, and that its most novel feature, the voluntary top-up payment, exists to let exporters demonstrate a higher effective carbon cost at home.
verbatim_quote: The regulation also introduces a new complementary carbon price mechanism, under which entities may voluntarily pay an additional amount on top of the price of allowances purchased at primary auction, a tool that could prove useful for exporters seeking to demonstrate a higher effective carbon cost paid at home.
verbatim_list: On 27 August 2026, Türkiye published secondary regulations for its national emissions trading system (TR-ETS) in the [Official Gazette]

The regulation defines the scope of the TR-ETS to cover Category B (50,000-500,000 tCO2​e) and Category C (>500,000 tCO2​e) installations across power and energy-intensive industrial sectors, while Category A facilities (<50,000 tCO2​e) remain subject only to MRV obligations.

The regulation establishes an intensity-based cap-setting framework, where the system-wide cap will be calculated ex post based on verified activity levels and benchmarks rather than being fixed in advance.

title: Carbon Leakage under CBAM and Free Allocation
date_evidence:
July 14, 2026

## Carbon Leakage under CBAM and Free Allocation
key_claim: ERCST and the Climate Economics Chair conclude that CBAM and free allocation are complementary rather than substitutable, that CBAM protects the EU market from imports but not exports, complex value chains or downstream sectors, and that CBAM should not replace free allocation until global carbon costs become more comparable.
frame_summary: ERCST is arguing that the gap between EU and non-EU carbon costs is wide enough and durable enough that the border charge cannot carry carbon-leakage protection on its own, which implies that recognition of foreign carbon prices will keep delivering only partial relief.
verbatim_quote: For policymakers, the conclusion is clear: CBAM and free allocation should be seen as complementary tools. CBAM is necessary, but it should not be treated as a full replacement for free allocation until global carbon costs become more comparable.
verbatim_list: CBAM is an important tool to protect EU industry from carbon leakage. It helps ensure that imports face a carbon cost when they enter the EU market.
notes: Used as the sourced counter-argument: the price gap, not the recognition test, may be the binding variable.

title: UK recognizes 16 overseas carbon pricing schemes for CBAM relief
key_claim: The UK government currently recognises 16 qualifying carbon pricing schemes for CBAM relief, including the EU ETS, China's national ETS, India's CCTS, Korea's K-ETS, Japan's GX-ETS and Australia's Safeguard Mechanism, with the list not exhaustive and kept under review.
frame_summary: EUROMETAL is arguing to a steel-trading readership that the UK list is commercially material because it determines which import origins can shed part of the UK border charge, and that it is provisional enough to be worth watching.
verbatim_quote: The government currently recognizes 16 qualifying carbon pricing schemes, including the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), China’s national ETS, India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), South Korea’s K-ETS, Japan’s GX-ETS and Australia’s Safeguard Mechanism.
verbatim_list: The amount of relief available will depend on the effective carbon price actually paid on the embedded emissions of the imported goods.
notes: Republished from the SteelOrbis Editorial Team; used for the count of 16 and for the trade-press read on materiality.

title: UK includes India's carbon credit trading scheme in list of qualifying carbon pricing mechanisms under CBAM
key_claim: HM Treasury wrote to India's Bureau of Energy Efficiency confirming that the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme meets the qualifying criteria under Part 3, Regulation 6 of the UK's 2026 CBAM relief regulations, following technical engagement between the Ministry of Commerce and its UK counterpart.
frame_summary: Reporting Commerce Ministry sources, the piece argues that recognition is the product of government-to-government technical diplomacy and is worth pursuing as an export-competitiveness win rather than a climate outcome.
verbatim_quote: In a communication addressed to the Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Ministry of Power, HM Treasury confirmed that the CCTS has been included in the UK’s published indicative list of overseas carbon pricing schemes, having been assessed as meeting the qualifying criteria under Part 3, Regulation 6 of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (Calculation of CBAM Rate and Determination of Carbon Price Relief) Regulations 2026.
verbatim_list: The recognition follows sustained technical-level engagement between the Ministry of Commerce and its UK counterpart on the design and implementation of the CCTS.
notes: Syndicated ANI copy carried by The Tribune. Used for the diplomacy limb of the signal.
